title: MSH — Message Header Segment
summary: The first segment of every v2 message — declares delimiters and identifies the message type.

elements.name: Field Separator
elements.description: Whatever character immediately follows "MSH" — conventionally |.

elements.name: Encoding Characters
elements.description: The other four delimiters in order: component (^), repetition (~), escape (\), subcomponent (&).

elements.name: Message Type
elements.description: Identifies the message type and trigger event, e.g. ADT^A01 — determines which segments follow.

elements.name: Accept Acknowledgment Type
elements.description: Negotiates original vs. enhanced acknowledgment mode with MSH-16.

elements.name: Application Acknowledgment Type
elements.description: Negotiates original vs. enhanced acknowledgment mode with MSH-15.

content.fieldNotes: No v2 message is valid without MSH as the first segment. Everything downstream — which delimiters are in force, what message type this is, how it gets acknowledged — is declared here before anything else is parsed.

title: ACK/NACK — Acknowledgment Model
summary: How every v2 message gets acknowledged — built around the MSA segment, with two negotiated modes.

elements.name: Acknowledgment Code
elements.description: AA/AE/AR (application) or CA/CE/CR (accept, enhanced mode only).

elements.name: Message Control ID
elements.description: Echoes the original message's control ID so the sender can match the ack to the message it acknowledges.

content.fieldNotes: Referenced by ADT, Orders, and Results alike — not owned by any one of them, which is why this is a relatedBlocks link from each rather than living under just one category. Mode matters in practice: in original mode, one ACK means done. In enhanced mode, a CA/CE/CR only confirms receipt — the sender still has to wait for a separate AA/AE/AR before treating the message as actually processed. Negotiated per-message via MSH-15/MSH-16.

title: EVN — Event Type Segment
summary: Carries the trigger event code and when it was recorded — the second segment in every ADT message.

elements.name: Event Type Code
elements.description: The trigger event, e.g. A01 — largely redundant with MSH-9 in practice but retained for backward compatibility.

elements.name: Recorded Date/Time
elements.description: System entry time — may lag the actual event. EVN-6 (when populated) is the more accurate "when it happened" timestamp.

content.fieldNotes: Don't assume EVN-2 tells you when the event actually happened — it's when the system recorded it. For clinical/billing accuracy, EVN-6 is the field that matters, and it's frequently unpopulated.

title: PID — Patient Identification Segment
summary: Carries patient demographic identity — the segment every ADT, Order, and Result message references back to.

sourceOfTruth.title: HL7 Version 2.5.1 Standard, Chapter 5 — Patient Administration

elements.name: Patient Identifier List
elements.description: One or more identifiers (e.g. MRN) for the patient — required, repeating.

elements.name: Patient Name
elements.description: Legal name and any aliases — required, repeating.

elements.name: Date/Time of Birth
elements.description: Optional, non-repeating.

elements.name: Administrative Sex
elements.description: Optional, non-repeating, coded value.

content.fieldNotes: PID-3 and PID-5 are the two fields every downstream system actually depends on — everything else on this segment is context, not identity. Missing or malformed PID-3 is the single most common cause of a failed patient match downstream.

title: PV1 — Patient Visit Segment
summary: Visit-level data — patient class, location, attending physician. Not patient identity; that's PID's job.

sourceOfTruth.title: HL7 Version 2.5.1 Standard, Chapter 5 — Patient Administration

elements.name: Patient Class
elements.description: I/O/E — inpatient, outpatient, or emergency.

elements.name: Assigned Patient Location
elements.description: Unit/room/bed.

elements.name: Attending Doctor
elements.description: Repeating — more than one attending is possible.

content.fieldNotes: Orders and Results both reference the visit context this segment establishes, alongside PID's patient context — this is the concrete mechanism behind ADT preceding Orders in the dependency graph, not just a convention.

title: NK1 — Next of Kin / Associated Parties Segment
summary: Next of kin / associated party information — optional and repeating, not part of the required ADT core.

sourceOfTruth.title: NK1 - Next Of Kin / Associated Parties Segment

elements.name: Set ID
elements.description: Sequence number, distinguishes repeats when a patient has multiple next-of-kin entries.

elements.name: Name
elements.description: Name of the associated party.

elements.name: Relationship
elements.description: Coded relationship to the patient.

content.fieldNotes: Optional and repeating in the base standard — zero, one, or many NK1 segments per message. Frequently made required by site-specific conformance profiles, but nothing else in this domain depends on it existing. Don't build an implementation that assumes it's always present.

title: ORC — Common Order Segment
summary: Fields common to every order type — order control, and the placer-side order identity shared with OBR.

elements.name: Order Control
elements.description: How the order is being created, cancelled, or modified (e.g. NW for new order).

elements.name: Placer Order Number
elements.description: Set by the ordering system. At least one of ORC-2/OBR-2 must be present; when both are present they should match.

elements.name: Filler Order Number
elements.description: Set by the fulfilling system — logically the same value as OBR-3.

content.fieldNotes: This is the segment that requires ADT's patient/visit context to already exist — an order is placed against a patient, not in isolation. Note: ORM^O01 (the traditional order message this segment lives in) was retained for backward compatibility only as of v2.4, withdrawn as of v2.7 — OMG/OML/OMD/OMS/OMN/OMI/OMP are the standard's actual direction from 2.4 onward, though ORM remains extremely common in real interfaces.

title: OBR — Observation Request Segment
summary: One segment definition, two jobs — order-group member in ORM, and report header in ORU. Genuinely shared, not duplicated.

elements.name: Placer Order Number
elements.description: Same identity function as ORC-2.

elements.name: Filler Order Number
elements.description: Logically the same value as ORC-3 — if ORC is absent from an ORU message, OBR-3 must carry it, since ORC is optional there.

elements.name: Universal Service Identifier
elements.description: What was ordered/performed — e.g. the test or panel.

content.fieldNotes: This is the deliberately shared node in the domain graph — carries the same tags as both Orders and Results, matching Cisco's duplicate-membership pattern (show ip route under both SHOW and ROUTE). One block, two collections, zero duplication. As a report header in ORU, it restates order context; the OBX segments that follow are what's actually new.

title: OBX — Observation/Result Segment
summary: One discrete observation — the smallest indivisible unit of a result report. Repeats once per measurement.

elements.name: Value Type
elements.description: The data type OBX-5 is formatted in — required whenever OBX-5 is populated.

elements.name: Observation Identifier
elements.description: Distinguishes multiple OBX segments carrying the same underlying test grouped under one OBR. Confidence note: sourcing on this specific data type (CE vs CWE) was ambiguous/contradictory across searches, unlike NK1-3 and OBR-4 which were clearly confirmed as CE — flagged, not silently asserted.

elements.name: Observation Value
elements.description: The actual measured/observed value, formatted per OBX-2.

content.fieldNotes: A single OBR can be followed by many OBX segments — one per discrete measurement the order produced. This is the FHIR analogue point worth remembering later: OBX generalizes into FHIR's Observation resource, but Observation covers more than OBX was ever built for (baselines, patterns, demographic characteristics, not just lab-style measurements).

title: FHIR RESTful Interactions
summary: The interaction set every FHIR resource type shares — read, create, update, delete, search — plus how a server declares what it actually supports.

elements.name: read
elements.description: Retrieve a single resource instance by id.

elements.name: search
elements.description: Retrieve a set of resources matching search parameters.

elements.name: create
elements.description: Server assigns a new logical id.

elements.name: update
elements.description: Replaces an existing instance.

elements.name: delete
elements.description: Removes an instance.

content.fieldNotes: Same interaction set applies uniformly to every resource type — that uniformity is what makes this its own capability rather than something re-explained per resource. A server's actual supported behavior is discoverable at runtime via its CapabilityStatement, not assumed from documentation alone.

title: GET [base]/Patient/{id}
summary: Retrieves a single Patient resource instance by its logical id.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: The resource's logical id, assigned by the server on create

content.fieldNotes: Same shape as a Cisco show command — a request and a real response — which is why this corner of FHIR stayed InvokableContent instead of needing the Structural shape the resources themselves required.

title: FHIR Terminology & Vocabulary Binding
summary: How coded elements on any resource get tied to external terminologies (LOINC, SNOMED) — referenced, not reimplemented.

elements.name: CodeSystem
elements.description: Defines a terminology's own codes — answers "what codes exist."

elements.name: ValueSet
elements.description: Selects a usable subset of codes from one or more CodeSystems for a specific purpose — answers "which codes are valid here."

elements.name: ConceptMap
elements.description: Maps between code systems inside FHIR's own terminology model, e.g. local code to LOINC. Does not translate v2 message semantics into FHIR resource semantics — that's a separate, still-open question (capability 10).

elements.name: binding strength: required
elements.description: The code must come from the indicated value set.

elements.name: binding strength: extensible
elements.description: Use the indicated set where it fits; codes outside it are permitted when nothing fits.

elements.name: binding strength: preferred
elements.description: A consensus recommendation, not an enforced constraint.

elements.name: binding strength: example
elements.description: Illustrative only — derived profiles may bind to any value set they choose.

content.exampleInstance: Observation.code bound to a LOINC-based ValueSet at 'extensible' strength
content.fieldNotes: Related to the resource-model overview by sequencing, not by hard technical dependency — you can understand CodeSystem/ValueSet without first knowing CRUD verbs, so this is a relatedBlocks link, not a prerequisite (Phase 5 note). SNOMED CT's restrictive licensing means the base FHIR spec predominantly uses it in example bindings, with occasional preferred-strength bindings — required strength is avoided specifically because of licensing, not as an absolute rule.

title: Patient
summary: The person receiving care — a standalone, referenceable resource, not a segment embedded in a message.

elements.name: identifier
elements.description: Business identifiers (MRN, SSN, etc.) — the FHIR analogue of PID-3, generalized to any identifier scheme.

elements.name: name
elements.description: Repeating — supports multiple names/aliases.

elements.name: gender
elements.description: Bound to a required-strength ValueSet — administrative gender, not clinical sex.

content.fieldNotes: Same identity function as v2's PID, but as its own addressable resource other resources reference by URL rather than a segment that only exists inside one message. `gender` here is administrative, not a clinical/biological claim — a common point of confusion worth calling out explicitly. Not every FHIR resource references Patient (Organization, Practitioner, CodeSystem, ValueSet don't) — it's specifically patient-context clinical resources that carry a subject/patient reference back to it.

title: Encounter
summary: Represents when and where care happened. FHIR treats care as happening inside an encounter.

elements.name: status
elements.description: planned | arrived | in-progress | finished | cancelled, etc.

elements.name: class
elements.description: Inpatient/outpatient/emergency-style categorization — the FHIR analogue of PV1-2's patient class.

elements.name: subject
elements.description: References the Patient this encounter is for.

elements.name: period
elements.description: Start/end of the encounter.

content.fieldNotes: Structural analogue of v2's PV1, but as its own standalone, referenceable resource rather than a segment living only inside a message. The subject reference is a soft link, not a hard prerequisite — you can understand Encounter's shape without first mastering Patient's internals, same as OBR referencing a prior order doesn't require re-deriving PID.

title: Observation
summary: A measurement or point-in-time assessment — the structural analogue of v2's OBX, generalized well beyond it.

elements.name: status
elements.description: registered | preliminary | final | amended, etc.

elements.name: code
elements.description: What was observed — coded, typically bound to LOINC. The direct analogue of OBX-3.

elements.name: value[x]
elements.description: The measured value — the analogue of OBX-5, with the data type expressed via the field name itself rather than a separate type field.

content.fieldNotes: Generalizes beyond what OBX was built for — baselines, patterns, and demographic characteristics, not just lab-style measurements. Observation.code is a coded element and genuinely benefits from understanding terminology binding, but that's recorded as a relatedBlocks link, not a hard prerequisite, for consistency with how the paradigm-vs-terminology edge was already softened elsewhere in this graph.

title: ServiceRequest
summary: A request for a procedure, diagnostic, or other service to be performed — the FHIR analogue of v2's order (ORC/OBR).

elements.name: status
elements.description: draft | active | completed | revoked, etc.

elements.name: intent
elements.description: Distinguishes order vs. proposal vs. plan — a distinction v2's ORC-1 order-control codes cover differently.

elements.name: code
elements.description: What's being requested — the analogue of OBR-4's Universal Service Identifier.

content.fieldNotes: Where v2 splits order identity across ORC and OBR, FHIR represents the whole request as one resource — worth flagging as a structural difference, not just a renaming, when capability 10 (v2-to-FHIR mapping) eventually gets researched.
